title: Iran Orders Houthis to Prepare Red Sea Blockade Threatening Saudi Oil Routes
excerpt: Tehran has instructed Yemen's Houthis to stand ready to close the Bab el-Mandeb Strait if the US strikes Iranian power infrastructure, deploying missiles and drones near the critical shipping chokepoint.
body:
• Iran has instructed Yemen's Houthis to prepare to shut down the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, the gateway to the Red Sea, if the US strikes Iranian power infrastructure
  • Houthis have deployed missiles and drones near the strait and await orders from IRGC representatives in Yemen to begin attacks on shipping
  • Saudi Arabia has redirected 70% of its energy exports through its Red Sea port of Yanbu after the Strait of Hormuz closure, making the Bab el-Mandeb route critical
  • A simultaneous disruption of both the Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb straits would shut down the Middle East's two main oil export routes, severely impacting Indian trade

Iran Orders Houthis to Prepare Red Sea Shutdown

Iran has asked Yemen's Houthi movement to stand ready to close the Red Sea oil route if the United States strikes Iranian power infrastructure, three sources told Reuters on July 16, posing a new and potent threat to global energy supplies already reeling from the Strait of Hormuz closure.

The message was conveyed recently to Tehran's Houthi allies through the Islamic Republic's leadership, according to two senior Iranian sources and a regional source familiar with the matter. A source close to the Houthis said the group had completed preparations to attack shipping by deploying missiles and drones near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a 20-mile-wide gateway between Yemen, Djibouti and Eritrea.

https://x.com/Fundji3/status/2078562982515359814

"If fighting intensifies and spills over into Red Sea export infrastructure and shipping, it will threaten the only major alternative route for oil exports from the region."

— Torbjorn Solvedt, Principal Middle East Analyst, Verisk Maplecroft

Representatives of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) who are already present in Yemen will control the decision on when to close the strait, the Houthi-linked source said. The IRGC has separately warned that "regional energy exports are either shared by all, or denied to all" — a statement analysts interpret as a direct reference to the Bab el-Mandeb.

Saudi-Houthi Truce Collapses After Four Years

Tensions between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia have flared sharply. On July 13, Yemeni government forces struck the runway at Sanaa International Airport to prevent an Iranian aircraft from landing. The Houthis retaliated with ballistic missiles and drones targeting Abha International Airport in southern Saudi Arabia, breaking a four-year truce that had held since 2022.

On July 16, Houthi leader Abdul Malik al-Houthi warned that Saudi oil facilities, ports, airports and other critical infrastructure would become missile and drone targets unless Riyadh "ceased and desisted." Two regional sources close to Riyadh said the kingdom was taking the threats from Iran and the Houthis seriously, aware that the Yemeni group was now closely coordinating with Iran over the Red Sea.

Double Chokepoint Crisis Threatens Global Oil

The strategic implications are severe. Since the Strait of Hormuz — historically the route for roughly one-fifth of global energy supplies — was shut after the US-Iran conflict erupted on February 28, Saudi Arabia has diverted approximately 70% of its energy exports through its Red Sea port of Yanbu. The Bab el-Mandeb route now carries around 7% of global energy supplies and approximately $1 trillion worth of goods annually.

Any Houthi attacks on vessels or ports in the Red Sea would leave both of the Middle East's main oil export routes disrupted simultaneously. Nadiya al-Dawsari, a Middle East analyst, noted that the Houthis "may not be able to fully close the strait, but they could significantly disrupt shipping and raise costs and risks for commercial traffic."

"Anybody with a firing rifle can interrupt the shipping. You don't have to have sophisticated missiles to interrupt the shipping."

— Regional source close to Riyadh, speaking to Reuters

India Faces Trade and Diaspora Fallout

For India, a dual chokepoint crisis carries direct consequences. The Red Sea and Suez Canal corridor handles a significant share of India's trade with Europe and the United States. When Houthis previously attacked shipping during the Gaza conflict in 2023-2024, major carriers rerouted around the Cape of Good Hope, adding two weeks and substantial costs to voyages. A renewed campaign would hit Indian importers and exporters hard.

Millions of Indian workers in the Gulf states — particularly in Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Bahrain and Kuwait — face heightened security risks as the conflict zone expands. Bahrain has already activated air raid sirens multiple times, and Kuwait has reported Iranian strikes damaging civilian infrastructure including power and desalination plants.

Brent crude rose back above $90 per barrel on July 20 for the first time since early June. With U.S. gasoline prices already up more than 30% since the war began, analysts warn that a Red Sea closure could push oil past $100 — compounding inflationary pressures on India's import bill and current account deficit.
image_caption: Satellite view of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, the narrow waterway connecting the Gulf of Aden to the Red Sea between Yemen and the Horn of Africa. Iran has instructed Houthi forces to prepare to block this critical shipping route.
